transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-08-04
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Ian Delgado (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Mistral CTO), Lydia Chen (Lead ML), Rajiv Mehta (Infra), Olivia Park (PM)

Summary (auto): Ian does a walkthrough of Redwood's JSON-mode with schemas and function calling. Priya shows Console flows and Optimize suggestions. Discussion covers VPC/private deployment questions, KMS, latency vs batching tradeoffs and next steps are pricing + security docs + benchmark window.

[00:00] Ian (AE): Hey everyone, great to meet you, thanks for carving time. Quick intros, we'll do a short context — what you run today — then dive into a structured output demo, func-call examples, and the Console/Optimize bits.
[00:23] Sam (Mistral): Hi, Sam here. We're mostly an analytics platform, real-time queries, low latency, and we need outputs that can be parsed deterministically into our metrics pipeline.
[00:34] Lydia: Yeah, our downstream system expects strict JSON, if it's malformed we lose signal and alerts blow up so it's a hard requirement.
[00:41] Priya (SE): Totally understood. We'll show JSON-mode with a schema validator and a guardrail layer that rejects or canonicalizes malformed outputs. We'll also show function-calling for entity extraction -> back-end enrichment flow.
[01:05] Rajiv: Quick infra note — do you do VPC peering or is it a VPN? We have strong policy about no egress to public internet for customer data.
[01:14] Ian: Good, this comes up a lot. We support Private deployments (VPC/On-prem) and VPC peering; Dedicated can be in your cloud with peering and private endpoints, and we can bring the control plane under customer networking in Private mode. We'll get the network diagram to you.
[01:34] Olivia: Also SOC2 — is your SOC2 in place and how about KMS? We need to know how keys are handled.
[01:40] Priya: We are SOC2 Type II. For Private/Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS or HSM, and we can do envelope encryption so keys never leave your control. I'll drop the SOC2 and KMS notes after the call.
[02:05] Ian: Alright demo start — I'm switching over to the Console. Note: the streaming toast may be laggy on my end. Apologies if that glitches.
[02:15] [screen share noise] Priya (SE): Here in the Console you can create a new Route, choose JSON mode, upload a JSON schema — here's an example schema for order events. Schema enforcement is optional or can be strict (fail responses) or lenient (attempt to repair). You can see an example guardrail policy we ship that rewrites certain fields or strips PII.
[02:46] Lydia: Can the schema allow multiple union types? sometimes our fields are string|array.
[02:52] Priya: Yes, we accept JSON Schema draft-07-ish unions; there are some runtime limits on extreme nested unions, we can show the Optimize recommendations for reducing complexity because that helps performance.
[03:20] Ian: Now switching to function calling, here's a simple flow: user prompt -> LLM returns structured JSON that includes a call to an extraction function with args -> Redwood invokes the function securely (we can do signed webhooks or an internal connector) and returns combined result.
[03:45] Sam: Wait, so the function calls are proxied through Redwood? or the model calls our webhook directly?
[03:50] Priya: Great question — we proxy the call through the Redwood control plane; you can configure the connector to use mutual TLS and IP allowlist so the webhook only accepts calls from our infra. For Private deployments the control plane can be on-prem or within your VPC so the call never leaves your network.
[04:15] Rajiv: How do you handle retries and idempotency for function calls — we can't have double-exec.
[04:22] Priya: We add an idempotency token and expose per-call status in the Console. There's a retry policy with exponential backoff and a dedupe window you can set.
[04:40] [06:00] Demo continued: We show a live prompt where the model is constrained by schema. Example prompt asks: "Extract top-3 entities and normalize timestamps" and returns a clean JSON payload.
[06:14] Speaker 2: (transcript glitch) "it returned like uh an array with a null but we can handle it" — some background noise.
[07:02] Priya: You'll notice there are two enforcement modes: BLOCK (reject response if schema doesn't validate) and REPAIR (attempt to coerce types and fill defaults). REPAIR uses deterministic rules you can customize in the Console.
[07:30] Lydia: If we choose REPAIR, will that mask model regressions and make tests flaky?
[07:36] Priya: Good point — that's why we pair REPAIR with alerts in Optimize. You get a quality dashboard and can set regression thresholds on schema mismatch rates; if REPAIR is happening frequently we'll surface an alert and suggest model or prompt changes.
[08:05] Ian: On the API side, the code snippet is straightforward: POST to /v1/generate with mode=json and schema_id=xxx, you can stream tokens but Redwood will assemble and validate final JSON before streaming out the validated object if you choose safe-streaming. That avoids partial JSON streams hitting your parser.
[08:40] Sam: Latency — we need sub-200ms median and 500ms tail for interactive sessions. How does batching/kv caching affect that?
[08:49] Priya: Latency depends on model choice and batching policy. Optimize will recommend a batching profile tied to your QPS distribution; for strict low-latency use a smaller batch target and enable prefix KV caching for repeated prompts. Dedicated pools can give you better tail performance due to isolation.
[09:25] Rajiv: If we go Dedicated, can we pin model versions and disable cross-tenant noisy neighbors?
[09:30] Ian: Yes, Dedicated lets you pin models and reserve GPU capacity. You get predictable throughput and can configure strict SLOs in the contract.
[09:45] [10:20] Priya: Now switching to a function-calling demo where the LLM returns an action: {"action":"create_ticket","args":{...}} — Redwood signs and forwards that call to a JIRA connector. We show audit logs in the Console with trace ids so every call is auditable.
[10:50] Lydia: How are audit logs retained and can we forward them to our SIEM?
[10:56] Priya: Logs can be exported to S3 or forwarded via secure syslog to your SIEM; retention policies are configurable per workspace.
[11:25] Ian: We'll highlight Optimize: it runs a static analyzer on your schema + prompts and suggests quantization profiles, batch sizes, and caching heuristics that reduce token cost with minimal quality regressions. It also suggests model candidates when it sees many schema repairs.
[11:52] Sam: Can Optimize run on historical traffic? like analyze our logs to propose different configs?
[11:58] Priya: Yes, if you share a sample trace or grant read-only access to the telemetry bucket, Optimize can simulate and give expected unit costs under different configs. That's what we typically do in pilots.
[12:30] [13:00] Interruption: minor audio drop for ~20s.
[13:25] Olivia: A question about function payloads — sensitive PII might be in the args, do you redact before logs?
[13:33] Priya: We have field-level redaction rules you can apply at ingress; the Console can redact and pseudonymize fields before they reach logs. For Private deployments you can also opt to not ship logs to Redwood's host and instead forward them to your S3 with zero copy.
[14:10] Lydia: Edge case — sometimes timestamps come in multiple formats, can schema coerce/time-normalize?
[14:18] Priya: Yes, we have canonicalizers and a small transform DSL to normalize timestamps, with built-in timezone heuristics.
[15:00] Ian: Let's walk through an end-to-end example: user question -> LLM returns structured plan with calls -> Redwood executes enrichment call to our connector -> returned enriched JSON gets validated and sent to your downstream. I'm going to paste the sample code and the schema in the chat (link).
[15:20] [chat link posted] "Console: https://console.redwood.ai/r/mistral/demo-schema"
[16:00] Sam: Looks good. One concern: double-commit risk on retry during function call failures, we need exactly-once semantics.
[16:07] Priya: For exactly-once, we recommend using idempotency tokens and making your connector idempotent keyed by request id; we can also support transactional connectors for certain integrations.
[16:40] Rajiv: About costs — if we do a test of 100k requests/day with JSON mode and repair on, what's the rough monthly?
[16:49] Ian: I'll send tiered pricing after this call but ballpark for JSON-mode generation + function-calls it's about 20-35% more than raw token generation due to validation and connector overhead; exact numbers in the deck.
[17:20] [18:00] Demo: Priya toggles strict enforcement and shows a rejected response sample with validation error code and trace id. The Console gives you a replay button to re-run request against a different model/temperature.
[18:40] Lydia: Nice, replay will help debug. Can we run A/B — call model A and fallback to B automatically?
[18:46] Priya: Yes, rollout policies allow canary, A/B, weighted, and automatic fallback when model latency or failure rates cross thresholds.
[19:20] Sam: Are there any examples of folks using this for billing reconciliation or financial normalized feeds?
[19:28] Ian: A couple of customers use JSON-mode + function-calling to normalize invoice lines for downstream billing engines. We can put you in touch with a reference.
[20:00] [20:40] Quick technical deep-dive: Priya gets into KV cache behavior and how it interacts with function calls — cache lookups are deterministic and prefix-based; function outputs can be cached only if the function is pure and you tag it as cacheable.
[21:12] Rajiv: For telemetry, can we get token-level breakdown per route?
[21:18] Priya: Yes, per-route / per-model token breakdown in Console, and you can export granular traces to BigQuery or S3.
[22:05] [23:00] Audience Q&A: Olivia asks about governance — role based access controls for who can add schemas or change repair rules.
[23:10] Ian: RBAC is supported — roles for schema editors, auditors, and ops. There's also an approval workflow for production schema changes.
[23:45] Lydia: Any limit on schema size? we have large nested objects.
[23:50] Priya: We support reasonably large schemas but recommend flattening extreme nesting, Optimize will flag complexity hotspots and we can suggest schema refactors.
[24:20] [26:00] Priya: Now a quick look at the Backend — runtime can choose optimized kernels and quantized models; we show an example compare: model-v1-xxf vs model-v2-q4 with similar quality on our eval set and much lower token cost.
[26:45] Sam: You said streaming safe-mode earlier, can you clarify?
[26:52] Priya: Safe-streaming will stream incremental tokens but withholds final validated JSON until validation ok; you can still see intermediate content in the Console but the SDK will deliver validated object to the app. This avoids parsing partial JSON.
[27:30] Rajiv: How do we test locally? do you have a dev SDK that simulates repair rules?
[27:36] Priya: Yes, the SDK includes a validator that runs your schema and guardrails locally; we also provide a replay tool to feed historical requests into Optimize.
[28:00] [29:00] Security deep-dive: Sam asks about key rotation and HSM. Priya explains support for customer-managed keys and HSM-backed KMS for Private.
[29:45] Ian: Ok let's talk logistics for the pilot — propose a 3-week pilot: week1 integration + sample data, week2 benchmark window, week3 evaluate results + contract talk. Does that timeline make sense?
[30:05] Sam: Yes that fits our timeline. We need the SOC2 packet and network diagram to start procurement.
[30:19] Ian: We'll send that. We'll also include a checklist for RPC/webhook allowlist and sample firewall rules.
[31:00] [32:00] Demo wrap: Priya runs a quick failure case where model returns wrong enum and repair rules coerce, plus an Optimize alert thrown into the evaluation queue.
[32:40] Lydia: Regarding monitoring, can we set a threshold on repair-rate and auto-roll back a route?
[32:46] Priya: You can set automated rollback policies tied to repair-rate or latency. The Console shows recommended rollback actions and you can wire a webhook for ops paging.
[33:20] Rajiv: A couple of nitty-gritty things: cert rotation for peering, ip ranges for egress during benchmark window, and if we can encrypt payloads at rest at field level.
[33:30] Priya: Cert rotation is supported; we'll share the ip ranges document. Field-level encryption is supported for Private via KMS transforms.
[34:05] [35:00] Wrap and recap: Ian: Action recap — we'll send pricing, SOC2 + network diagram, sample schema eval set, and propose the pilot dates. Priya: I'll own the security packet and the runbook for the benchmark. Sam: We'll get sample payloads and confirm pilot approvers.
[35:35] Olivia: One last ask — can you provide a short example notebook that shows the SDK integration for streaming+function-call?
[35:42] Priya: Yes, we'll attach a Colab / GitHub gist.
[36:00] [37:00] Quick FYI — roles and stakeholders listed in chat for procurement.
[37:20] Ian: That should be everything on our side, any final Qs?
[37:27] Sam: No other questions, looks good. We're excited to try the pilot.
[37:40] Lydia: Thanks everyone.
[37:50] Ian: Thanks — we'll follow up via email with the packet and pricing.

End notes: Shared links in chat: Console demo link, sample schema, security packet placeholder.

Post-call notes (auto): transcription contains some small mis-attributions and a couple of timing gaps around 13:00 due to audio dropout. Quality flagged as medium.
